title: Ocular Needle Stick Injury: Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) Protocol
summary: A comprehensive clinical guide for the immediate management of percutaneous or mucocutaneous exposure to blood-borne pathogens (HIV, HBV, HCV) in the ophthalmic setting. Rapid risk stratification and timely PEP initiation are critical to preventing seroconversion.

sections.title: Immediate First Aid (The First 60 Seconds)
content: 1. Percutaneous Injury: Wash the site immediately with soap and water. Do not scrub excessively; avoid caustic agents like bleach.
2. Mucocutaneous/Eye Splash: Flush the eyes/mucosa with saline or sterile water for at least 15 minutes using an eyewash station or irrigating solution.
3. Reporting: Notify your supervisor or Occupational Health department IMMEDIATELY to establish a baseline and documentation.
4. Source Assessment: Attempt to identify the source patient's status (HBV, HCV, HIV) through chart review or rapid testing if consent is obtained.

sections.title: PEP Red Flags & Timing
content: PEP must be initiated within 1-2 hours of exposure.
Delay beyond 72 hours renders PEP likely ineffective.
Never wait for source patient lab results before starting PEP if risk is high.
Assess for drug-drug interactions (e.g., antiretrovirals vs. common eye drops/anticoagulants).

sections.title: HIV PEP Regimen: The 3-Drug Gold Standard

content.explanation: T (Tenofovir), H (History of Source), E (Emtricitabine/Eyewash), 3 (3-drug regimen for 28 days).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls for Ophthalmic Surgeons
content: Use 'Hands-Free' technique for passing sharp instruments in the OR.
Double-gloving has been shown to reduce blood-to-skin volume in percutaneous injuries.
HCV Post-Exposure: There is no post-exposure prophylaxis for Hepatitis C. Monitor for seroconversion and refer to GI if ALT/PCR indicates infection.
Psychosocial Support: Exposure often leads to significant anxiety; provide counseling resources as standard of care.
